ta-l1d26q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 26. Having treated essence and persons, Lombard now treats the properties by which the persons are distinguished: first the properties proper to the persons, then those appropriated to them (Dist. 31). The proper properties are personal ones (Dist. 26–27, with a comparison of names signifying the persons in Dist. 27) and non-personal properties of the persons (Dist. 28). On personal properties he first treats the hypostasis, which underlies the properties as the distinct underlies the distinguishing, then the properties by which hypostases are distinguished, assigning their number and mode of predication (relatively, not substantially, accidentally, or temporally, but from eternity). He then removes doubts about the Son's property and the Spirit's, as Gift and as Holy Spirit, and excludes the error that 'Holy Spirit' or 'Gift' is not said relatively. Thomas asks first about hypostasis, then about properties; on hypostasis, whether it is in God and what it signifies, and whether hypostases remain distinct when the personal properties are abstracted by the intellect.
claims: Hypostasis underlies the properties as the distinct underlies the distinguishing.
Personal properties are predicated relatively and from eternity.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e134.summary: First argument that 'hypostasis' should not properly be said of God. Jerome in the text says the name is not of good repute and that poison lies hidden under honey.
claims: Jerome distrusts 'hypostasis'.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e137.summary: Second argument. Boethius says hypostasis names a substance underlying accidents, and God underlies no accident (Augustine, Dist. 8).
claims: Hypostasis underlies accidents.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e140.summary: Third argument. Hypostasis names a thing of a nature (res naturae) standing under a nature, and in every such thing the nature seems simpler, the thing adding something to it, or else one nature would mean one thing of nature. Where there is addition there is composition, so every hypostasis is composite, and there is no composition in God.
claims: The res naturae adds to the nature, implying composition.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e144.summary: Fourth argument. Every hypostasis is a subsistence and essence, since whatever stands under subsists and is. So a divine hypostasis would be a subsistence and essence, yet we say three hypostases but not three essences or subsistences (Boethius).
claims: Hypostasis implies subsistence and essence.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e147.summary: Fifth argument. Everything in God is absolute or relative. Hypostasis is not absolute, since nothing absolute is distinguished in God (Augustine, Boethius), and hypostasis is; nor relative, since relation is the distinguishing and hypostasis the distinguished.
claims: Hypostasis is neither absolute nor relative.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e150.summary: Sixth argument. The indeterminate relates to the determinate as possible and material, and person relates to hypostasis as determinate to indeterminate, or distinct to distinguishable, since a person is a hypostasis distinguished by a property of dignity. Nothing in God is material, potential, or incomplete.
claims: Hypostasis is indeterminate relative to person.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e153.summary: Sed contra. As said in Dist. 25, the Greeks mean by hypostasis what we mean by person, which is properly said of God, plurally of the three and singularly of each.
claims: Hypostasis corresponds to persona.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e156.summary: Thomas's determination. Among the Greeks hypostasis is principally the individual of substance, our first substance: something complete, distinct, and incommunicable in the nature of substance. So the divine hypostasis is what subsists through itself, distinct and incommunicable. Nothing absolute is distinct in God, only the relative, and as the essence is the very thing that is, the distinguishing relation is really the distinct itself. Since relation is really the same as essence, what is distinct by relation is really the same as what subsists in the divine nature, and that is what 'hypostasis' signifies. So 'hypostasis' in God signifies relation as distinct by way of a subsistent in the divine nature, as with 'person'. But 'hypostasis' does not include a determinate character of distinction, while 'person' includes a special one pertaining to dignity, as subsisting in a noble, intellectual nature, though Greek usage gives 'hypostasis' this too (Boethius). 'Father' further signifies the distinct by expressing the special, determinate character of distinction, the relation of paternity. So the four follow in order: hypostasis is a subsistent distinct in any way; divine hypostasis a subsistent distinct by relation, since there is no other distinction in God; person a subsistent distinct by a relation pertaining to dignity; Father a subsistent distinct by the relation of dignity that is paternity.
claims: 'Hypostasis' in God signifies relation as distinct by way of a subsistent in the divine nature.
Hypostasis, divine hypostasis, person, and Father are progressively determinate.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e159.summary: Reply to the first argument. The Latin word corresponding to 'hypostasis', 'substance', is equivocal between essence and first substance, so to avoid deception Jerome would not use 'hypostasis' before its meaning was known and settled, lest heretics deceive the simple by arguing from distinction of hypostases to distinction of essence.
claims: Jerome's caution was pastoral, avoiding confusion with essence.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e163.summary: Reply to the second argument. Although in reality nothing in God is under another or underlies another as an accident, something is understood to underlie as to mode of signifying, as Damascene says some names in God signify what follows the substance, like goodness, wisdom, paternity, and so 'hypostasis' can be said there.
claims: God underlies properties only in our mode of signifying.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e166.summary: Reply to the third argument. Hypostasis in God is a thing of a nature. An individual substance is so called either by underlying a nature or by underlying accidents and properties, and each can be signified by a first-intention or a second-intention name: as underlying a nature, 'thing of nature' (res naturae) and 'supposit'; as underlying a property, 'hypostasis' or 'person' and 'singular' or 'individual'. The last two are not properly in God, since they express a determinate mode of distinction through matter; 'incommunicable' is used instead. The nature need not be simpler than the thing of nature, since in simple things the quiddity is the simple thing itself (Avicenna), differing only in mode of signifying, quiddity as form and the thing as subsistent. Distinction among things of the nature comes not from the nature but from the opposed relations subsisting in it.
claims: In simple things the nature is the thing itself, differing only in mode of signifying.
Res naturae and suppositum signify the subsistent as underlying the nature; hypostasis and persona as underlying the property.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e169.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. As said in Dist. 25, the person in God is distinguished not by nature or being but only by properties, so names said with respect to property are predicated plurally (hypostasis, person) and names said with respect to being singularly (subsistence, essence), though the saints use 'subsistence' for hypostasis. Some names refer to the common nature and are also plural (res naturae, supposit), since although they do not refer to the property as form, they name something distinct under the common nature and so signify the relations as subsistent. Subsistence and essence do not name something distinct, and so are prior in genera and species than in individuals (Boethius), and properly taken are not predicated plurally, as among the Greeks.
claims: Names relating to property, or naming something distinct under the nature, are plural; names relating to being are singular.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e172.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. 'Hypostasis' in God signifies relation by way of substance. As by simplicity essence and being are the same in God, so are the distinguishing relation and what is distinct by relation, but they differ in mode of signifying, which is grounded in reality, since each name has its true signification in God. So they differ in supposition too: as we say God begets and deity does not, we say the hypostasis is distinguished and the relation distinguishes.
claims: The distinguishing relation and the distinct hypostasis are really the same but differ in mode of signifying and supposition.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e175.summary: Reply to the sixth argument. 'Person' and 'hypostasis' both signify something distinct in God, but 'person' determines a special mode of distinction, by a noble property, which 'hypostasis' does not, so they are like superior and inferior, as some substance is more common than some man. In composites this determination and indetermination of common and proper reduces to the material and formal in reality, since genus flows from matter and difference from form, but in simple things there is nothing indeterminate in reality, as material, determined by a supervening form, only in mode of signifying, since both names truly signify in God.
claims: Hypostasis and person are related as superior and inferior only in mode of signifying in God.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e187.summary: First argument that, with the relations removed by the intellect, the hypostases remain distinct. Augustine says in everything said relatively there is something said absolutely, since a related thing is not only related but something. So if hypostasis is said by relation, there is something subsistent understood besides the relation, which remains when the relative properties are removed.
claims: Every relative is also something absolute.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e190.summary: Second argument. Hypostasis is more perfect in God than in creatures, and in creatures, with the relation of one hypostasis to another removed in thought or reality, the hypostases remain, like Socrates and Plato.
claims: Creaturely hypostases survive removal of relations.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e193.summary: Third argument. Whatever falls in a definition can be understood without what it is defined with, as animal without rational. A person is a hypostasis distinguished by a property of dignity, so with the relative property removed the distinct hypostasis remains.
claims: Hypostasis, as part of the definition of person, can be understood without the property.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e197.summary: Fourth argument. The Father has being someone (quis) and being Father, from the same or from different things. If from the same, since he is Father by paternity, he would be someone by paternity, and the Son, lacking paternity, would not be someone, which is false. So it is from something else, which remains when paternity is removed, and 'someone' names the hypostasis.
claims: Being 'quis' cannot come from paternity.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e200.summary: Sed contra. Augustine says Father and Son are one in everything except what is said relatively, so with the relation removed only what unites them remains, which cannot be distinct. Boethius likewise says relation alone multiplies the Trinity.
claims: Only relation multiplies the Trinity.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e203.summary: Thomas's determination. Some say that, as in creatures hypostases remain distinct by themselves when relations and properties are removed, so in God, and that with personality, the relation constituting the person, abstracted, the hypostasis remains. This cannot stand given the faith, for two reasons. First, plurality is always caused by distinction, and all distinction is by essence, quantity, or relation, so in God there can be no distinction but what relation causes, and removing the relations removes the very concept of distinction. Second, nothing in God is predicated as an accident or as a form inhering in something pre-existing, so whatever is signified as a form is wholly subsistent: as removing the essence leaves nothing receiving it, since the essence subsists, and removing goodness leaves nothing receiving it, so removing a relation leaves nothing underlying it, since the relation is itself a subsistent thing. So, properly speaking, with the relation abstracted nothing remains, neither absolute nor related, neither hypostasis nor essence. Still, the essence can be understood without goodness being understood (Boethius), and without paternity or relation being understood, as the Jews understand it, but not by way of abstraction. One cannot understand a relation removed in God with something subsisting beneath it, since the relation itself subsists there. So, with others, Thomas grants that with the relation removed no distinct hypostasis remains in God, both because no distinction remains and because nothing remains underlying the relation. But if the relations the faith distinguishes had never been, God would be both substance and person, as subsisting in his being and underlying essential properties by which he would be distinguished from other essences.
claims: Abstracting the relations, no distinct hypostases remain in God.
In God only relation distinguishes, and what is signified as form is wholly subsistent, so nothing underlies the relation.
Without the relations God would still be one person, by subsisting and by essential properties.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e206.summary: Reply to the first argument. In God there is both absolute and related, but relation does not come to the absolute as distinguishing it; it is identical with it in every way. What is distinguished by relation is the relation itself, which can be signified as subsistent, and so it is signified by 'person' or 'hypostasis'.
claims: What relation distinguishes is the relation itself, signified as subsistent.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e209.summary: Reply to the second argument. In creatures hypostases are distinguished by matter, and diverse properties show the distinction, but in God they are distinguished only by relation, since the only real otherness there is relative opposition. So as in creatures hypostases do not remain distinct when the division of matter and quantity is removed in thought, in God they do not remain when relative opposition is removed.
claims: Removing the principle of distinction removes the distinct hypostases, in creatures as in God.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e212.summary: Reply to the third argument. Hypostasis is placed in the definition of person because person adds something to hypostasis, not relation, since relation is of the concept of divine hypostasis as of person, but a determinate character of relation pertaining to dignity. So with the relation removed neither hypostasis nor person remains in God, and since a divine hypostasis is already posited as subsisting in a noble property, the nobility that 'person' adds is included in 'divine hypostasis'. As a human hypostasis says no less than a person, neither does a divine hypostasis.
claims: A divine hypostasis already includes the nobility that 'person' adds.

ta-l1d26q1-d1e216.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. By paternity the Father has both being someone and being Father, but it does not follow that the Son is not someone, since what paternity is for the Father, filiation, also a relation, is for the Son. With relation abstracted, neither Father nor Son is someone, but each is someone by his own relation, as each is a person by his own personality, and one's personality is not the other's, as explained in Dist. 25 on the commonness of person.
claims: Each person is 'someone' by his own relation.

ta-l1d26q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 26 introduces Lombard's treatment of the properties distinguishing the persons, beginning with the hypostasis underlying them, then the personal properties and their mode of predication, with doubts about the Son and the Spirit. It announces two articles on hypostasis: whether it is in God and what it signifies, and whether hypostases remain when the properties are abstracted.
claims: Hypostasis underlies the distinguishing properties.

ta-l1d26q1-Dd1e126.summary: Article 1 holds that hypostasis is in God and signifies relation as distinct by way of a subsistent in the divine nature, since only the relative is distinct in God and the distinguishing relation is the distinct itself. Hypostasis, divine hypostasis, person, and Father are progressively determinate. Jerome's caution about the word was pastoral; God underlies properties only in our mode of signifying; in simple things the nature is the thing of nature itself; names relating to property or to something distinct are plural, those relating to being singular; and the relation and the hypostasis differ only in mode of signifying.
claims: 'Hypostasis' in God signifies subsistent relation as distinct.
Hypostasis and person differ only as less and more determinate in mode of signifying.

ta-l1d26q1-Dd1e179.summary: Article 2 holds, against those who make God like creatures here, that with the relations abstracted no distinct hypostases remain in God. Only relation distinguishes in God, and whatever is signified as form in God is wholly subsistent, so nothing underlies the relation. The essence can be understood without the relations, as the Jews do, but not by abstraction; and were there no relations, God would be one person by subsisting and by essential properties. Each person is 'someone' by his own relation.
claims: Removing the relations removes the distinct hypostases in God.
Relations in God have no substrate; they subsist.

ta-l1d26q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 26 treats the hypostasis. Article 1 holds that 'hypostasis' is properly said of God and signifies relation as distinct by way of a subsistent in the divine nature, ordered with divine hypostasis, person, and Father as progressively determinate, and differing from relation only in mode of signifying. Article 2 holds that, since only relation distinguishes in God and the relations themselves subsist without substrate, abstracting the relations leaves no distinct hypostases, though without them God would be one person.
claims: 'Hypostasis' in God signifies subsistent relation as distinct.
Abstracting the relations, no distinct hypostases remain.
